media.alt: Experts stress global health must incorporate new models of health professional education

content.text: As society and its medical challenges evolve globally, we need new models of health professional education that straddle multiple disciplines and geographic boundaries, said Dr Robert Armstrong of the Aga Khan University and colleagues, in a "perspective" in this week's Science.

Historically, public health professionals have been largely trained as clinicians with expertise in infectious disease prevention while the training of doctors has focused on disease and curative approaches to health problems with little interaction and often distrust between the schools. But this is leading to poor adaptation and loss of leadership opportunity in the face of existing and emerging challenges that are rooted in a complex web of medical, socioeconomic, religious and cultural issues.

In Models of education in medicine, public health, and engineering, Dr Armstrong, Dean of AKU's Medical College in East Africa, Dr Patricia Garcia from the School of Public Health and Administration, Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia in Peru, and Dr Muhammad H Zaman from Howard Hughes Medical Institute, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Boston University, USA argue that an interdisciplinary and systems approach to training is needed.

Global health is not about developed countries helping to solve the problems of the developing world but about having the global capacity to tackle challenging issues, the solutions to which can drive innovation and opportunity in both directions said Dr Armstrong.

The need for rethinking medical education has been echoed in several high-level reports, including the 2010 Lancet Commission on Health Professional Training for the 21st Century, which argues for major reforms across the entire health professional education system with competency based curriculum, systems thinking and global perspectives closely linked to health and health care delivery systems.

The Aga Khan University in East Africa is developing such an innovative undergraduate programme, integrating the training of nurses and doctors and equipping them with the knowledge, skills, behaviors and attitudes that will prepare them to tackle the problems of East Arica and contribute new knowledge to the challenges we face as a global community.

AKU and the University of Toronto have also begun testing new models for courses that bring together students from various disciplines across geographic boundaries using blended learning strategies. The goal is to expose students to the richness of global issues and to encourage collaborative curriculum development that captures the expertise of faculty across disciplinary and geographic boundaries.

The current trial links 4th-year undergraduate science and arts students at the University of Toronto with advanced nursing students in Tanzania and Uganda and education students in Pakistan in a common course that relies on case-based problems built around a shared resource.
With the right focus, the innovations occurring in health professional education will produce a new type of graduate, one who can reach out globally to tackle the issues of concern locally.
